titre: The Edict of Milan (313): A Letter From Licinius, Posted at Nicomedia
accroche: The text called the “Edict of Milan” was not published in Milan, is not by Constantine alone, and is not an edict.
contenu_vulgarise:
“The Edict of Milan of 313” appears in almost every textbook: Constantine, having become a Christian, grants freedom of worship to the Empire. Yet no document bears this name, and the one that comes closest was not published in Milan.

## What Has Actually Been Preserved

The starting point is earlier. On April 30, 311, the emperor Galerius, on his deathbed, had an edict of toleration posted at Nicomedia, dated from Serdica, which ended the persecution of the Christians. Two years later, in February 313, Constantine and Licinius, masters respectively of the West and of part of the East, met in Milan. There they settled, according to the sources, the affairs of state, among them religious policy.

The text that is called the “Edict of Milan” is something else. After his military victory, Licinius entered Nicomedia and had posted there, on the Ides of June, that is, June 13, 313, a letter addressed to the governors of his eastern provinces. Lactantius, a contemporary Christian rhetorician, copies it in Latin at the end of his *De la mort des persécuteurs* (On the Death of the Persecutors). Eusebius of Caesarea gives, in his *Histoire ecclésiastique* (Ecclesiastical History), a Greek translation whose wording differs noticeably. Neither version has the form of an edict: it is a letter of instruction, and the original letters themselves have not come down to us, only these quotations.

What does it say? That everyone has the freedom to follow the religion he judges best, that Christians may remain in theirs without hindrance, and that the free exercise of their cults is likewise granted to all others. It also orders the restitution, without payment, of the places of worship confiscated from Christians, those who had acquired them or received them as gifts being able to request compensation from imperial funds.

## What This Shifts

As early as 1891, the German historian Otto Seeck disputed that there had ever been an “Edict of Milan.” This thesis has become, according to current syntheses, the dominant view among specialists: the expression is a construction of church history.

The shift lies in what was believed to be read. Toleration is not an act of Constantine alone: the preserved text is Licinius's, addressed to his own governors. And it is addressed to all: the text does not make Christianity the religion of the Empire, it ends its persecution and also covers cults that are not Christian. The passage from a tolerated religion to a favored one is another episode, and remains to be told elsewhere.

repere.texte: The text called the “Edict of Milan” is a letter from Licinius to the governors of the East, posted at Nicomedia on the Ides of June 313. Lactantius preserves it in Latin; Eusebius of Caesarea gives a Greek version with differing wording. Otto Seeck disputed as early as 1891 that an Edict of Milan had existed.
repere.source: Lactantius, De la mort des persécuteurs (On the Death of the Persecutors), ch. XLVIII; Wikipedia, Edict of Milan

carte.punch: The “Edict of Milan” is not an edict, and was not published in Milan.
carte.idee: The 313 text attributed to Constantine is a letter from Licinius to the governors of the East, posted at Nicomedia on June 13. Lactantius gives the Latin version, Eusebius a divergent Greek version. Otto Seeck already doubted it in 1891.

quiz.question: Why do specialists consider the expression “Edict of Milan” misleading?
choix: The text was written by Constantine alone, several years after 313
The preserved text is a letter from Licinius posted at Nicomedia, not an edict published in Milan
The text imposes Christianity as the official religion of the Empire
The text is a forgery composed in the medieval period
quiz.explication: The text is a letter from Licinius to the governors of the East, posted at Nicomedia. It was not written by Constantine alone, does not make Christianity mandatory (it grants freedom of worship to all), and we have it from Lactantius and Eusebius, two contemporaries.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who preserves the Latin text of Licinius's letter?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Lactantius copies it at the end of his De la mort des persécuteurs; Eusebius gives only a Greek translation. Galerius is the author of the 311 edict and Seeck a historian of 1891.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the letter provide for the places of worship confiscated from Christians?
choix: They are converted into imperial temples, with no compensation for anyone
They are restored without payment, with possible compensation for the purchasers
They remain state property, which the state now administers
They are bought back by the bishops, at a price set by the emperor
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The letter orders restitution without payment, those who had bought or received these properties being able to turn to the emperor for compensation; it leaves them neither to the state nor to the bishops to buy back.
